transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (SE), Sam Huang (SE), Mark Rivera (CTO, AtlasAI), Lina Zhang (ML Eng), Jorge Ramos (Infra), Aisha Patel (Product)

Summary:
- Quick review of pilot week 2 results (INT8 vs FP8 vs FP16 baseline).
- Discussed sensitivity failures, a small cluster of high-regret queries, and an adaptive routing playbook to fallback to full precision on risky inputs.
- Agreed actions: 24h soak, share telemetry, provide security docs, schedule SLA/pricing call.

Topics:
- Perf deltas (throughput/latency/cost)
- Quality impact by slice (classification recall, hallucination cases)
- Routing/playbook for adaptive precision and canary rollout
- Networking/VPC and compliance checklist
- Next steps and owners

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: okay everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to keep this tight 45 to 60, quick sync on the quant pilot, uh week two results. Priya and I will walk through the numbers, then open for Qs.
[00:28] Mark: thanks alex, quick context, we're really focused on customer-facing summaries so throughput matters but recall on our classification labels can't drop more than about 1.5 percentage points overall.
[01:05] Priya: got it, we tuned for that. high level: INT8 gave ~1.7x tokens/sec vs your FP16 baseline and FP8 is around 1.9x on your A100s, latency p50 improved ~20% for both. cost per token estimate dropped by ~35% (INT8) and ~42% (FP8) in our cost model.
[01:45] Jorge: can you remind me those numbers are with continuous batching on? we saw some weird p tail during our tests.
[02:10] Priya: yes continuous batching was on; we used a small max batch size 12 because of your 200ms tail SLO. the tail increases when batch sizes spike, we instrumented to limit spikes.
[02:48] Lina: quality—where are we on recall? any slices that look bad?
[03:12] Priya: overall recall dropped ~1.1% on INT8, FP8 was ~0.6% drop. but we found a 2.8% drop on one user intent slice (short, highly templated prompts with punctuation oddities). that's the high-regret cluster.
[03:45] Alex: yeah that cluster is the key; we think it's a tokenization + prompt-padding interaction — small prompts with trailing spaces get slightly different token alignments after quantization kernels, which amplifies logits noise.
[04:10] Mark: interesting, so it's not the model per se but an edge effect of tokenization + quant?
[04:32] Priya: right, and that maps to the set Lina flagged. our suggestion is an adaptive routing playbook: route those short templated prompts to FP16 (or a fallback FP32 variant) and keep most traffic on INT8/FP8.
[05:00] Aisha: how would we detect those on the fly? we don't want to add latency for classification at the front.
[05:25] Priya: two options — lightweight regex tags or a micro-classifier (cheap binary model) in front. regex is easiest: detect < 30 tokens and unusual punctuation pattern, tag for fallback. micro-classifier adds small cost but better precision.
[05:50] Alex: we also support a hybrid: run regex first, if ambiguous, do a tiny prefix-check model that runs on CPU < 10ms. it's part of the routing playbook we can ship.
[06:20] Jorge: for the VPC pilot what changes? we need to test peering and the egress IP allowlist.
[06:45] Sam: we'll coordinate with you — Redwood will request a peering window and provide firewall IPs. there may be ephemeral ranges for autoscaling but we provide a stable egress set for pilot.
[07:10] Mark: about fallbacks — what's the cost delta when you fallback to FP16 for a slice? is it a big hit?
[07:30] Priya: fallback to FP16 increases cost for those requests by ~2.3x compared to INT8. but because the high-regret slice is small (we estimate ~4% traffic), net platform cost still ends ~15-18% below baseline with adaptive routing.
[08:05] Lina: accuracy-wise, does FP8 ever outperform INT8 on our prompts or is it just throughput?
[08:28] Priya: FP8 tends to give slightly better fidelity on low magnitude logits in some cases — that's why we saw lower recall drop versus INT8 on that templated slice. it's not consistent, which is why playbook and per-slice policies help.
[09:02] Mark: ok good. any hallucination differences? we've had a few halluc cases in production.
[09:25] Priya: hallucination rate was flat within noise for both INT8/FP8 vs FP16; the regression we saw was mostly label flip in short prompts, not stochastic hallucination.
[09:55] Alex: moving to rollout mechanics — our recommended canary is 5% traffic, monitor recall and latency for 24h, then 25%, 50% ramp with automatic rollback if recall drops >1.2% or p95 latency spikes >40%.
[10:30] Jorge: do you have telemetry hooks we can wire into our datadog?
[10:48] Sam: yes we emit metrics and traces; we'll share a telemetry spec. we can stream per-request flags for the high-regret tag and precision used.
[11:12] Mark: what about KV cache warming and cold-starts? some of our flows have long contexts.
[11:35] Priya: KV cache behaves normally; quantized kernels have slightly different warmup characteristics — cold-starts see ~10% perf hit for first 2 tokens while caches populate. we recommend short warmup bursts or synthetic warmup traffic for high-latency flows.
[12:05] Lina: are there any model compilation steps we need on our side? e.g., changed operators?
[12:30] Priya: no changes to your model artifacts. Redwood compiles and selects kernels in the runtime; for Private deployments we provide the pre-compiled bundles. there can be small operator mismatches for custom ops — we saw none in your model.
[13:00] Mark: security checks — SSO, KMS, audit logs — are those ready for pilot?
[13:20] Alex: yes, we have an enterprise pack: SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS hooks, and request-level audit logs. we'll share the security whitepaper and a network diagram after the call.
[13:45] Aisha: timeline — if pilot goes well we'd want dedicated next quarter. do you have baseline SLA targets?
[14:05] Alex: we can propose a pilot SLA for availability 99.9 and p95 latency target aligned to your current SLOs; dedicated contract options include tighter SLAs and reserved capacity.
[14:30] Lina: we ran a local ablation last night and saw that zero-shot prompts degrade more than template-based ones when quantized. any mitigations?
[14:55] Priya: yes zero-shot tends to be more fragile — we recommend routing zero-shot-like prompts to FP8 instead of INT8, or using a small calibration set to bias logits.
[15:22] Mark: do you support gradual precision mixing per endpoint? like adaptive precision by route?
[15:45] Sam: yes the platform supports per-route precision policies; you can set rules by header, prompt tag, or a micro-classifier signal. those rules are evaluated in the smart router before the request hits the mesh.
[16:10] Jorge: how much overhead does the router add?
[16:30] Priya: router evaluation is ~1-3ms for regex rules, ~8-12ms if you use the micro-classifier. in practice this is hidden by batching for bulk paths; we accounted for it in the latency budget.
[16:55] Aisha: curious — any concerns about vendor lock with this routing approach? we want to keep portability.
[17:20] Alex: the policies are declarative and stored in your config; you can export them. the core runtime is Redwood-specific but we keep the policy layer portable as JSON.
[18:00] Mark: what about rollback playbooks? if we see regressed metrics during canary can we auto-fallback to baseline model?
[18:22] Priya: yes automatic fallback is supported: triggers can be metric-based or manual. we can set an automatic rollback to FP16 for any failing slice.
[18:50] Lina: curious about tokenizer variance — can we pre-normalize prompts?
[19:10] Priya: absolutely, we've seen normalizing trailing whitespace and punctuation fixes that templated slice. we can provide a tiny preproc lib.
[19:40] Mark: ok, let's talk about the soak you mentioned — what's in scope?
[20:00] Alex: 24h soak with adaptive routing enabled, include telemetry for high-regret tag, run at traffic parity with production 4% sample, compare recall/latency and cost deltas.
[20:25] Lina: we'll provide the query dump, how will you handle PII?
[20:40] Alex: please mask PII before upload; we accept redaction or hashing. we also support on-prem ingestion if you prefer.
[21:05] Jorge: networking — we need the IP ranges and peering window.
[21:25] Sam: we'll post the network diagram and stable egress block and propose a peering window next Tuesday.
[21:50] Aisha: any legal items? we have a procurement checkpoint next month.
[22:10] Alex: we'll surface standard terms and the pilot contract; procurement folks can review.
[22:35] Mark: competitors — Megacloud AI pitched an all-managed approach but their latency numbers were optimistic. OpenServe offered a cheaper FP8-only lane but lacked the adaptive fallback.
[23:00] Priya: yep that's consistent; our differentiation is the routing + observability for precision mixing.
[23:20] Alex: quick risk checklist — slices to watch: short templated prompts, zero-shot prompts, and long context cold-starts. we'll instrument all three.
[23:50] Lina: thanks. would like to see the per-slice confusion matrix after the soak.
[24:10] Priya: we'll produce per-slice precision/recall and confusion matrices, plus per-route latency breakdown.
[24:40] Mark: what telemetry access will we get? read-only dashboards?
[25:00] Sam: we'll give read-only dashboards and API keys for pulling raw metrics; we can also set up a datadog integration.
[25:20] Alex: last section — operational playbook snippet. we propose: 1) canary 5% with regex routing for known templated prompts, 2) monitor for 24h, 3) if recall drift > 1.2% auto rollback, 4) if stable move to 25% then 50%.
[25:55] Jorge: sounds good. how do we tag requests to track routing decisions?
[26:15] Priya: every request gets metadata: route_precision, high_regret_flag, batch_id; we stream those fields to your telemetry.
[26:40] Aisha: one more ask — can you share a quick script to reproduce the quantized run locally so our infra team can sanity-check?
[26:58] Priya: yes we'll share a minimal reproducible recipe that runs on a single node and simulates batching and kv-cache warmup.
[27:18] Mark: rough timeline — if soak passes we want to move to dedicated eval in Feb. is that realistic?
[27:38] Alex: yes if soak and network checks look good, dedicated evaluation in Feb is feasible.
[28:00] Lina: are there any vendor-specific compile flags that change behavior?
[28:20] Priya: runtime picks fastest kernels; on some hardware we preselect alternate kernels for FP8. we'll document the flags — nothing you need to change unless you run private bundles.
[28:45] Sam: i'll put the kernel selection doc in the binder.
[29:05] Mark: okay let's recap next steps.
[29:20] Alex: recap: Redwood: upload bench spreadsheet + cost model, enable routing on staging, share telemetry spec and security whitepaper; Atlas: provide 500 masked high-regret queries, confirm peering window, review pilot contract.
[29:50] Aisha: who owns the pilot runbook? want a single doc we can iterate.
[30:05] Alex: Alex will own the runbook and Priya will own telemetry instrumentation. we'll set it up in the shared drive.
[30:30] Mark: any outstanding technical blockers?
[30:45] Priya: not blockers — just the tokenizer edge and zero-shot sensitivity which we can mitigate via routing.
[31:05] Jorge: one operational note: autoscaling could change egress ranges during pilot — can you pin egress to a stable prefix?
[31:25] Sam: yes for pilots we can allocate a stable egress block to avoid firewall churn.
[31:45] Lina: Perf question: can we tune batch sizes dynamically per route?
[32:05] Priya: yes we support route-level batching policies, so you can keep interactive routes low-latency and bulk routes large.
[32:30] Mark: ok solid. anything else?
[32:45] Aisha: procurement will need the pilot T&Cs.
[33:00] Alex: we'll send a pilot addendum and an outline of charges for fallback usage.
[33:20] Priya: small note — for the micro-classifier option we can provide a prebuilt binary you run in your infra to avoid extra network hops.
[33:45] Jorge: that might be useful for low-latency paths.
[34:00] Alex: perfect. feel like we have a path forward. thanks everyone.
[34:18] Mark: thanks all.
[34:30] (call wraps; detailed Q&A followed in chat but not recorded in transcript)

End of transcript.
